posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: Hi everyone! Whenever people say LEGO is "just a toy for kids," I love showing them what happens when you combine mechanical engineering, geometry, and a few thousand Technic bricks! ⚙️🧱 I’d like to share my project currently live on LEGO Ideas: the Working Analog Clock. The main challenge was creating a fully functional, two-handed clock where the movement isn't driven by a standard center axle, but by concentric ring gears driven around a virtual center. The Engineering Behind the Build: To make this concept a reality, I had to solve a few major hurdles that went way beyond "just stacking bricks": Virtual Center Mechanics: Driving two massive concentric rings (built using Technic Curved Gear Racks 24121) without a physical central axle required an independent vertical suspension system for each ring to keep friction minimal while maintaining precise alignment. The "Ghost Hand" Dilemma: To keep standard clock proportions (where the shorter hour hand floats in front of the minute hand), I engineered an internal transfer link—a "Ghost Hand"—that routes the movement from the rear hour ring forward to a smaller front indicator. Single-Drive Synchronized Reduction: Scrapping early dual-motor prototypes, the entire mechanism is now synchronized through a single, compact gear reduction train housed in the rear chassis. Why Share This Here? Eurobricks is one of the best places for deep-dive technical feedback, so I’d love to know your thoughts: How do you usually handle friction and structural roll when dealing with large, suspended Technic rings? What do you think of using an internal transfer arm ("Ghost Hand") vs. mounting hands directly onto the outer rings? If you'd like to see the full evolution, technical updates, or support the build, check out the official LEGO Ideas page! 👉 https://ideas.lego.com/projects/09f27699-c246-40a3-8eea-9a0867d1470f Looking forward to your thoughts, constructive suggestions, and ideas for discussion!

posts.title: LEGO Star Wars Set Discussion 2026 - READ FIRST POST!!!
posts.text: I agree with you in every regard. Of course, as you said, nowadays the non-minifigure sets have furiously expanded to licensed themes, too. Though there were the Technic sets and a few other "gimmicks" back in the old days, too, like Belville and some others, which were not compatible with the Lego System universe. So there are fans and audience for them, too, I should not deny it, but TLG should not underestimate the magic of the universality underlining a lot of their success. Even for a 100% collector the universal compability enables creative displays of one's own choosing. Statues and other collector items are much more purely collector items, which in most cases lack this feature entirely. I find particularly the Friends line a massive improvement, which was a huge hit mostly because it made the girls' and boys' universes compatible in a way, which is much more interesting for example siblings playing together. I remember when I was a young kid in 90s that I was confused why my Lego figures seemed like shrunken men in my sister's and her friends' Belville universum, when we played together.

posts.title: LEGO Star Wars Set Discussion 2026 - READ FIRST POST!!!
posts.text: As much as I attribute this problem to those running the Lego Star Wars theme, I equally blame Lucasfilm for seemingly not caring enough to apply a little bit of pressure on Lego as a licensee to stop disregarding the new stuff they put out. Lego is the only toy licensee who actively ignore new Star Wars content yet are fine experimenting with countless objectively bad ideas. Experimentation is fine, but don’t lose the forest for the trees. Yeah I struggle to imagine how the slightly juvenile nature of the Ewoks (which is overblown IMO) could outweigh the final act of the film and Anakin’s return to the light. What I really like about both the OT and PT is how much you can see the characters growing through each film because of the time gaps. For the OT especially I remember as a kid noticing how much Luke changes from ANH (naive and starry eyed) through TESB (cocky and slightly arrogant) to RotJ (wise and measured). Given that NYCC is approaching, it would’ve been the perfect time to debut the 50th Anniversary sets. For all my disappointment as of late, I still think it’s absolutely awesome that full-blown January waves are a thing again. The most ironic thing (and I say this as someone who tries to see the positives) is how Smart Play brings literally nothing new to the table outside of the Smart Brick itself. The figures / characters aren’t new, the sets are just inferior rehashes of things that have been done before with the exception of a pretty damn good Falcon, and yet Lego are actively throwing so many slots at it at the cost of normal playsets. Ironically I haven’t seen the 18+ portfolio take a hit to accommodate Smart Play too which makes me more annoyed. The moat for regular playset fans continues to shrink. I completely agree, however the spirit of Lego System rooted in minifigures and builds that are agnostic of theme and are endlessly compatible doesn’t hold the prevalence it used to. Prior to the mid-late 2020’s, it was mostly unheard of for licensed sets not to involve minifigures or minidolls as a focus, whereas now it’s commonplace that buildable characters and objects are very much an acceptable substitute. I do find it sad because System is and always will be the soul of Lego, but it’s no longer the core of the brand the way it used to be when it comes to licensed themes.

posts.title: YuzuLingo - Browser extension for hover OCR & dictionary lookups on hardcoded subtitles (YouTube, Bilibili, etc.)
posts.text: I'm the developer of YuzuLingo and wanted to share a free browser extension I built to help with watching Chinese dramas and videos when soft subtitles aren't available. If you stream Chinese shows on YouTube, Bilibili, or older TV platforms, a lot of content still relies on hardcoded (burned-in) Chinese captions. Standard popup dictionaries like Zhongwen or Yomitan can't capture text inside video frames, leaving you to manually type out characters or pause constantly. YuzuLingo runs local on-device hover OCR directly over the web video player frame. Whenever you hit a character or fast line in hardsubs, you can hover over the text on screen to get instant pinyin, definitions, and popups. You can also export words straight to Anki to keep flashcard creation fast while mining shows. It works directly in Chrome and Firefox. You can check it out here: YuzuLingo. I'd love to hear any feedback or feature requests from fellow learners using it for their watch routines!

posts.title: Online Chinese stories in English
posts.text: Two resources match your method (read it in English first, then find the Chinese) better than a plain list of story sites does: 1. ctext.org (Chinese Text Project) - for classical texts it shows the Chinese original next to a translation, and often links several translations of the same passage, so you can see exactly where they disagree. 2. zh.wikisource.org together with Project Gutenberg - the same public-domain work usually exists in both places, one in Chinese and one in English. Concrete pairs that work well: - 聊斋志异 <-> Herbert Giles, Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio - 诗经 <-> James Legge's translations (both on ctext.org) - 老残游记 <-> The Travels of Lao Can (Gutenberg) - 阿Q正传 <-> Yang Xianyi's translation One warning about the English-first approach: the free translations above are free because they are old. Giles and Legge wrote a hundred years ago, their English is dated and they take real liberties with the original - Legge even keeps the Chinese word order in places. Read them for the story, but do not use them to learn how a modern translator handles a sentence. For modern fiction the problem is the other way round: the Chinese original is usually easier to find than an authorised English translation, so 活着 or 平凡的世界 are easier to enter from the Chinese side than from the English side.

posts.title: 梓 zǐ — how did an ordinary catalpa tree become THE name character of the 2010s? Does it feel dated now?
posts.text: There's a naming phenomenon in mainland China I keep running into: for roughly a decade, 梓 zǐ — the catalpa tree, a fairly ordinary hardwood traditionally planted by the house — became arguably the single most popular character in newborn names (梓涵, 梓萱, and hundreds of variants). The character has respectable roots, to be fair: 梓 was literally the tree of home (桑梓 still means hometown), and it also referred to the wooden blocks used for printing, hence printing plates in old publishing contexts. So it is not a shallow pick. But I'm curious about the felt sense for native speakers in 2026: when you hear 梓 in a name now, does it read as the generational default, the way English speakers hear Jennifer or Jayden? Is the wave already cresting, and if so, what character do you sense filling the same slot next?

posts.title: 静好 jìng hǎo — feminine-only, or does the Book of Songs float free of gender?
posts.text: A client brought me 静好 (jìng hǎo) last week — she'd found it in the Book of Songs, from the line 琴瑟在御，莫不静好 ("with qin and se in hand, all is calm and good"). It's a genuinely lovely pull: two characters, both gentle to write, good visual balance stacked vertically on skin. My question for native speakers: does 静好 read strictly feminine to you? The client is a woman so it's fine here, but I keep wondering — if a man asked for it, would it raise eyebrows, or is it one of those literary phrases that floats free of gender? Also curious whether it reads as a plausible given name, or more like a phrase someone lifted straight out of a poem. Grateful for any native instincts on this.

posts.title: Not sure if that tattoo was a good idea
posts.text: Coming at this from the needle side rather than the language side, so treat the scholarship as a second opinion. What makes a Chinese-character tattoo read as "native" or not is usually not the meaning. It is mostly three things: whether the characters are cut at a consistent size, whether each character is balanced inside its own square (Chinese characters want to sit in a square, and Japanese-influenced lettering often stretches them taller and lets strokes run from one character into the next), and whether the client chose a complete phrase or a fragment. 歲寒知松柏 is a full classical line, which is the safer kind. The ones that quietly get laughed at are usually two adjectives stacked side by side that do not actually pair up grammatically. For what it is worth, "will Chinese people find this funny" is the wrong thing to be haunted by. The question I would ask instead is whether the same four characters still say something to you in ten years, because that is the only part of a tattoo that is genuinely permanent. The same test applies to the single characters people pick for names. I always set a candidate in a square seal before anything goes on skin, and plenty of beautiful ideas turn into a black blob at the size they actually get reproduced at. If it survives the seal, it survives everything.

posts.title: Native-speaker feedback on a Chinese name for a children's space-builder hero
posts.text: Chiming in from a slightly different angle than everyone else here — I'm not a native speaker. I'm a tattoo artist in the US, and most of my work with Chinese is visual: I look at how a name carries weight on the skin and how much story one character can hold. So take this for what it's worth. Something I don't think has been raised yet: kids' franchises live and die on a single character. The full name will be in the theme song and the credits, but what ends up on the chest, the toy box and the sticker sheet is one big character, usually the one in the middle. So it's worth asking which single character in each candidate can carry the whole concept on its own. On that front, 匠 is the most interesting one in this whole thread. It's 斤 (an axe) inside 匚 (a box) — literally a craftsman's toolbox. It's one of the few characters on the table where the picture still matches the meaning, and "a maker with his tools" is exactly the concept you described. 创 reads as "create" but the shape is abstract, and 建 is construction vocabulary, as Silver2333 said. So my vote is whichever option puts 匠 or 创 in the load-bearing position and treats everything before it as a prefix. 星匠侠 is a genuinely good find for that reason. One practical note from my side of the fence: test the name at seal size. A lot of otherwise fine names turn into an unreadable blob once you set them in a red square seal, and that's the asset that gets reused everywhere — merch, avatars, end cards, promotional art. If a name survives a seal, it survives a toy box.

posts.title: 对酒当歌 — natural for casual use, or strictly literary?
posts.text: Tattoo artist and long-time lurker here. Over the past couple of months, two different clients asked me to ink the line 对酒当歌 from Cao Cao's 短歌行. I enjoy writing it in seal script — the round, heavy strokes suit the wistful, slightly drunk mood of the poem. Before I recommend it to the next person, I'd like to check the register with people who actually use the language: would quoting 对酒当歌 in a casual setting — a toast at dinner, a social media caption — sound natural to a native speaker, or does it land the way quoting Shakespeare does in English, i.e. clearly literary? I'm not worried about the meaning itself, more about whether everyday use would come across as pretentious or out of place. If there are modern songs or shows that use the phrase, that would help me gauge the register too. Thanks in advance!

posts.title: TianTian (天天): HSK photo flashcards with audio, as a phone web app. Feedback welcome
posts.text: Hi everyone, this is the team behind TianTian, introducing our product here as the forum policy asks (one post, this subforum only). What it is: a phone web app (PWA), so there's nothing to install from an app store; you open it in the browser and add it to your home screen. It's built around photo flashcards with native audio and spaced repetition, plus HSK 1 grammar lessons with practice, a sentence builder (tap the words in the right order), listening drills and short Reading texts you can tap to hear. Premium can download all audio and pictures for offline use; on the free plan, audio streams online and the words you've already played stay cached. The free plan needs no sign-up. The interface is English/Portuguese because we started with Brazilian learners, who have very few resources in their own language. Where it honestly stands today: HSK 1 is complete and follows the classic 150-word list (HSK 2.0). HSK 2 and above are still being built and will be added level by level. It isn't a dictionary or a reader, so Pleco and graded readers still do their own jobs alongside it. Pricing: the free tier includes 20 words per level (with ads). Premium unlocks everything and removes ads: about US$3.99/month, US$24.99/year or US$49.99 lifetime, charged in your local currency by card at checkout. Where we'd really value this forum's experience: 1. Photos for abstract HSK 1 words (的, 了, 是, 会 vs 能): do our images help, or would you rather see example sentences for those? 2. Audio: is it clear and natural enough, and should we add slow-speed playback? 3. With HSK 3.0's first official exam on 13 December 2026 (300 words at level 1), would you expand HSK 1 to the new list first, or build HSK 2 on the classic list first? 4. Is the sentence builder too easy at HSK 1? https://tiantianhsk.com/?utm_source=chineseforums&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=launch&utm_content=intro We'll answer every reply in this thread. Thanks for taking a look, and for being blunt.
